title: Levi's table (Mark 2:13–17)
hook: the healthy don't need a doctor; he came for sinners
carry: the doctor is for the sick

segments.voice: Yesterday, four men dug through a clay roof and lowered their paralytic friend to Jesus. Your line was friends who dig through roofs. Did you find the stairs for someone? Day one hundred sixty-four.

Some towns have one person everybody agrees is on the wrong side. Not a criminal, exactly. Just the one nobody wants at the barbecue. In Capernaum that man sat in a booth by the road, taking tolls. His name was Levi. Jesus walks past the booth and says: follow me. And Mark says, just like that, he got up and followed. Then comes the part that really starts the gossip. There's a dinner at Levi's house. It fills with his friends, the ones decent people crossed the street to avoid. And Jesus sits down with them. Today we pull up a chair at Levi's table.
screen: `A TOLL BOOTH BY THE ROAD.` → `FOLLOW ME.` → `A HOUSE FULL OF THE WRONG PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Tax collectors in Galilee gathered tolls and duties on goods moving along the roads, for Herod's government, which answered to Rome. They were widely suspected of taking extra for themselves, and neighbors could see them as working for the occupier. So when the old King James Bible says Jesus sat down with "publicans and sinners", it means people who were written off. Publicans is the old word for tax collectors. And in that world, eating with someone wasn't a small thing. A shared table said: we belong together. Some scribes of the Pharisees see it and ask the disciples, why does he eat with these people? It's a fair question in their world. They cared deeply about holiness, and holiness has a lot to do with who you let close. Jesus overhears, and answers with a picture anyone can understand: "They that are whole have no need of the physician, but they that are sick: I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." A doctor who only visits healthy people isn't much of a doctor. Christians hear a few things in this. Some hear good news for anyone who feels too far gone: the table is set for exactly those people. Others hear a gentle question for the ones who feel healthy: are you sure? And one more detail. Matthew's gospel tells the same story and calls the tax collector Matthew. Christian tradition has long taken Levi and Matthew to be the same man, so the toll collector may be the one whose name is on a gospel.
screen: `TOLLS, AND A BAD NAME.` · `A SHARED TABLE MEANT BELONGING.` · `THE DOCTOR IS FOR THE SICK.` · `LEVI, ALSO CALLED MATTHEW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat with someone unlike you. Not today, necessarily. First, find them. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people you'd never quite sit with: a coworker from the other side of an argument, a neighbor you've made up your mind about, a relative who votes differently. Pick one face. Notice what happens in your chest when you picture sharing a table with them. Don't fix it. Just notice. Then imagine the meal anyway: what you'd order, what you might ask them. If you pray, you can hold that person before God for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Levi's table. A tax collector's dinner, full of people nobody wanted, and Jesus in the middle of it.
Your line: the doctor is for the sick. Today, set a place, even a coffee, even a lunch break, for someone you'd usually eat apart from. Day one hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Many churches remember Levi's dinner in shared meals open to anyone, such as community suppers and food programs, and Christians often point to this passage when welcoming people who feel unwelcome elsewhere.

original.note: Greek: a collector of tolls and duties; the Latin publicanus gave the King James its publican.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice dinner party in the Bible.
what it means: a despised toll collector hosts the people nobody sits with, and Jesus eats with them.
what a scholar hears: in that world a shared meal meant belonging, so the table itself was both the scandal and the point.

sources.quoted: They that are whole have no need of the physician, but they that are sick: I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens 'Think of'; 'says two words: follow me' varied (day 159 used it); 'Levi throws a dinner' softened to a dinner at his house (Mark 2:15 is ambiguous; Luke 5:29 says Levi made the feast); 'many' claims softened.
Tolls in Galilee under Herod Antipas (a client ruler under Rome): confirm the phrasing 'for Herod's government, which answered to Rome'.
Pharisees are presented as caring about holiness, with a fair question; confirm tone.
Levi = Matthew is a traditional identification (Matthew 9:9), stated as tradition; some scholars doubt it. Confirm.
Original: τελώνης; confirm pronunciation guide and the publicanus link.
